notes.meaning: A severe famine struck the land for three years in a row, leading David to ask God why it was happening. The Lord revealed that the famine was a judgment because King Saul had broken Israel's ancient promise and slaughtered the Gibeonites. Unrepented national sin can bring long-lasting trouble until the wrong is faced and settled.

David called the Gibeonites together to address the wrong done to them. The Gibeonites were not Israelites, but Israel had sworn a solemn covenant in Joshua's day to protect them. Saul had ignored that sacred oath and attacked them out of misguided zeal for Israel and Judah.

David asked the Gibeonites how he could make amends, or provide atonement, to right the wrong. Atonement here means covering over the sin so it is removed from view. David wanted them to be fully satisfied so they could ask the Lord to bless Israel again.

The Gibeonites made it clear that money could not pay for the loss of human life, nor did they want to harm ordinary Israelites. Under biblical law, bloodguilt required life for life from the family responsible. David then promised to do whatever they justly requested.

The Gibeonites described how Saul had plotted to wipe out their people from the land of Israel. They asked for seven male descendants of Saul to be handed over and executed publicly before the Lord in Saul's hometown of Gibeah. David agreed, knowing that public justice was needed to satisfy God's law and end the famine.

David protected Jonathan's son Mephibosheth and would not give him up. David had made a sacred promise to Jonathan before the Lord to show kindness to his family forever. Even while correcting Saul's broken oath, David faithfully kept his own covenant.

David chose two sons of Saul born to his concubine Rizpah, and five grandsons born to Saul's daughter Merab. These seven men were selected to answer for the royal family's crimes against the Gibeonites. Even when leaders fall, the painful consequences of their sin often spill over into the lives of their families.

David handed the seven men over to the Gibeonites, who executed them on a hill before the Lord. This happened in early spring, right at the start of the barley harvest. The public execution showed everyone that God holds all people, even kings, accountable for shed blood.

Rizpah showed great love and grief by spreading sackcloth on a rock near the bodies of her sons. She stayed there day and night for months, keeping predatory birds and wild animals from touching them. Her vigil continued until the rains poured down from heaven, proving that God's anger was satisfied and the famine had ended.

David was told about Rizpah's faithful watch over the dead bodies. Hearing of her deep grief and loyalty touched the king's heart with great pity. A faithful act of love can soften hearts and inspire others to do what is right.

Stirred by Rizpah's devotion, David went to retrieve the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead. The brave men of that town had rescued those bodies after the Philistines hung them on the wall at Beth-shan. David wanted to give Saul's family the honorable resting place they deserved.

David brought back the bones of Saul and Jonathan, along with the remains of the seven men who had recently been executed. He gathered all these family members together so they could be buried properly. This showed that David acted out of obedience to God, not personal malice against Saul's house.

All the remains were buried together in the tomb of Saul's father, Kish, in the territory of Benjamin. After the king and his people carried out everything God required, God heard their prayers and healed the land. When sin is fully confessed and set right, God graciously restores His favor.

War broke out once more between the Philistines and Israel. David led his soldiers down to fight, but the aging king became weak and exhausted in the battle. Even the greatest warriors of faith eventually face human limits and need help from others.

A giant named Ishbi-benob, a descendant of Rapha, saw that David was weak and tried to kill him. This warrior carried a heavy bronze spear weighing around seven and a half pounds, and he had armed himself with a new sword. Enemy forces often attack most fiercely when they see God's servants grow weary.

Abishai rushed to David's side, struck the giant, and killed him. David's men then swore that he must never go out to battle again, so that the 'lamp of Israel' would not be put out. They saw David as the light guiding the nation's peace and God's kingdom on earth.

Later on, another battle with the Philistines took place at Gob. In that clash, Sibbecai the Hushathite, one of David's mighty men, struck down another giant named Saph. God raised up new champions among the people so that Israel's victory did not depend on David alone.

In another battle at Gob, Elhanan from Bethlehem killed the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was as thick as a weaver's beam. The parallel record in 1 Chronicles clarifies that this victim was Goliath's brother Lahmi. God continued to give David's soldiers the courage to overcome the fiercest enemies.

In yet another battle at Gath, a huge giant with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot taunted Israel. David's nephew Jonathan, the son of Shimei, went out and struck him down. Just as David had silenced Goliath years earlier, his family members now stepped forward in faith to silence those who defied God.

These four giant warriors of Gath all fell before David and his faithful soldiers. The passage closes by showing how David's leadership inspired a whole group of courageous men to conquer their foes. God gives His people victory over giant problems through unity, faith, and enduring courage.
